glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus, Timothy is to pass Paul’s teaching on to faithful people, endure hardship for the risen Christ, handle the word of truth rightly, keep himself clean for the Master’s use, and correct opponents gently in the hope that God will grant them repentance.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: “You therefore, my son” (2:1) follows the contrast between those who turned away from Paul and Onesiphorus, who stood by him (1:15–18). Paul is in chains, and teachers such as Hymenaeus and Philetus are overthrowing the faith of some (2:9, 17–18).

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “You therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. And the things that you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit these to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:1–2)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Chapter 1 told Timothy to guard the gospel. Chapter 2 tells him to hand it on and to suffer for it, beginning with a strength he does not have to produce: “be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” (2:1). That grace also sends the teaching onward: Paul to Timothy, Timothy to “faithful men,” and those men to “others also” (2:2). The soldier, the athlete, and the farmer each picture service that costs something and leads to a reward (2:3–6).

At the center Paul places a person: “Remember that Jesus Christ, of the seed of David, was raised from the dead” (2:8). Paul wears chains for that gospel, “but the word of God is not chained” (2:9). The faithful saying then draws believers into Christ’s own path through death into life. Those who died with Him will live with Him, and those who endure will reign with Him, yet “If we deny Him, He also will deny us” (2:12). The last line begins, “If we are faithless,” and then rests everything on Christ Himself: “He remains faithful; He cannot deny Himself” (2:13). He will do what He has promised, and He will do what He has warned.

The rest of the chapter concerns how God’s word is handled. Quarrels about words ruin those who hear them (2:14), and the claim of Hymenaeus and Philetus that “the resurrection is already past” is overthrowing the faith of some (2:18). Yet God’s foundation stands, and whoever cleanses himself becomes a vessel “useful for the Master” (2:19–21). The chapter ends with the Lord’s servant, who corrects opponents gently in the hope that God will grant them repentance and free them from “the snare of the devil” (2:24–26). Error is to be answered in a way that seeks to rescue the person who holds it.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
2 Timothy 2:1–2 — Strong in Grace and Entrusting the Teaching

Paul tells Timothy, his son, to draw his strength from Christ’s grace rather than from his own resources. The teaching Timothy heard from Paul, confirmed among many witnesses, must now be committed to faithful people who will be able to teach others.

2 Timothy 2:3–7 — The Soldier, the Athlete, and the Farmer

Timothy must accept hardship as a good soldier of Jesus Christ, who keeps free of entanglements so that he may please the one who enlisted him. The athlete who competes by the rules and the hardworking farmer who shares first in the crops complete the picture, and Paul asks Timothy to think them through while the Lord gives him understanding.

2 Timothy 2:8–10 — Remember the Risen Christ and the Unchained Word

Paul points Timothy to Jesus Christ, David’s descendant, raised from the dead and standing at the center of the gospel Paul preaches. Paul is chained for that gospel, yet God’s word is not chained, and he endures all things so that God’s chosen people may obtain salvation in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.

2 Timothy 2:11–13 — The Faithful Saying

A trustworthy saying in four lines promises that those who died with Christ will live with Him and that those who endure will reign with Him, and it warns that those who deny Him will be denied by Him. Its last line begins, “If we are faithless,” and rests the whole saying on Christ, who remains faithful and cannot deny Himself, so He will do both what He promised and what He warned.

2 Timothy 2:14–18 — The Approved Worker and the Spreading Error

Timothy must charge believers not to fight about words, which ruins those who listen, and he must work to be approved by God, handling the word of truth accurately. He must shun empty, godless talk, which spreads like cancer, as it has through Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection is already past and are overthrowing the faith of some.

2 Timothy 2:19–21 — God’s Firm Foundation and Vessels for Honor

Despite that spreading error, God’s foundation stands, sealed by the Lord’s knowledge of those who are His and by the call for all who name Christ to depart from iniquity. Like a household vessel kept for honorable use, whoever cleanses himself becomes set apart, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work.

2 Timothy 2:22–26 — The Lord’s Servant Who Corrects with Gentleness

Timothy is to flee youthful lusts and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with others who call on the Lord from a pure heart. The Lord’s servant avoids quarrels and corrects opponents with gentleness and patience, hoping that God will grant them repentance so they may know the truth and escape the devil’s snare.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Second Timothy 2 shows how God keeps His truth alive from one generation to the next: through ordinary, faithful people who receive the teaching and hand it on to others (2:2).

The faithful saying guards against two dangers at once (2:11–13). Christ is true to His promise and true to His warning. Saving faith endures, and a settled, final denial of Christ meets His denial. Yet Peter, who denied Jesus and was restored, shows that a believer who falls still has room to repent (Luke 22:54–62; John 21:15–19). Read as one whole, the saying leaves no room for careless confidence or for despair.

The way truth is defended also matters to God. The Lord’s servant must be “gentle to all, able to teach, patient” (2:24), because correction aims at an opponent’s repentance and freedom rather than at winning the argument.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Grace that strengthens. Timothy’s endurance draws on Christ’s grace, and Paul endures so that others may obtain salvation (2:1, 10).

Passing on the truth. The teaching moves from Paul to Timothy to faithful people who will teach others (2:2, 14).

Enduring with Christ. Hardship and labor for the gospel look ahead to life and reign with Christ (2:3–6, 10–12).

The word handled rightly. Accurate handling of the word of truth stands against empty talk that spreads like cancer (2:15–18).

Gentleness that seeks repentance. The Lord’s servant corrects opponents patiently, hoping that God will grant them repentance (2:24–26).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Faithful men (2:2). Reliable people who will keep Paul’s teaching intact and are able to teach it to others.

Of the seed of David (2:8). A descendant of King David. The phrase ties Jesus to God’s promise of a lasting kingdom for David’s line (2 Samuel 7:12–13).

The elect (2:10). The people God has chosen. Paul endures suffering so that they may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus.

This is a faithful saying (2:11). Paul’s way of introducing a trustworthy statement. Its four “if” lines belong together and should be read as one whole.

Rightly dividing the word of truth (2:15). Handling God’s word accurately. The Greek word pictures cutting a straight line, the way a careful worker does a job he will not be ashamed of. It does not mean splitting the Bible into separate parts.

Vessels for honor (2:20–21). Household containers set apart for honorable use. To cleanse oneself “from the latter” (2:21) includes departing from iniquity (2:19) and rejecting the corrupt teaching Paul has just described (2:16–18).

focus: Second Timothy 2 turns the charge to guard the gospel into a charge to pass it on and endure for it. Strengthened by grace and anchored in the risen Christ, Timothy is to entrust Paul’s teaching to faithful people, accept hardship, handle the word of truth rightly, keep himself clean for the Master’s use, and correct those in opposition with gentleness in the hope that God will grant them repentance.

sections.title: Strong in Grace and Entrusting the Teaching
sections.summary: Paul tells Timothy, his son, to “be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 2:1). The things Timothy heard from Paul among many witnesses he must commit to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

sections.title: The Soldier, the Athlete, and the Farmer
sections.summary: Timothy must endure hardship as a good soldier of Jesus Christ, for a soldier keeps himself from becoming entangled in the affairs of this life so that he may please the one who enlisted him. The athlete who competes by the rules and the hardworking farmer who shares first in the crops complete the picture, and Paul tells Timothy to consider these things while praying that the Lord will give him understanding in all things.

sections.title: Remember the Risen Christ and the Unchained Word
sections.summary: Paul calls Timothy to remember that Jesus Christ, of the seed of David, was raised from the dead according to Paul’s gospel. For that gospel Paul suffers chains as if he were an evildoer, yet “the word of God is not chained” (2 Timothy 2:9), and he endures all things for the sake of the elect so that they also may obtain salvation in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.

sections.title: The Faithful Saying
sections.summary: This faithful saying offers two promises and a warning: those who died with Christ will live with Him, those who endure will reign with Him, and “If we deny Him, He also will deny us” (2 Timothy 2:12). Its fourth line, “If we are faithless, He remains faithful; He cannot deny Himself” (2 Timothy 2:13), rests the whole saying on Christ’s own character, so that He stays true both to His promises and to His warning.

sections.title: The Approved Worker and the Spreading Error
sections.summary: Timothy must remind those he teaches of these things and charge them before the Lord not to strive about words, to the ruin of the hearers, while he himself works to be approved by God, “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). He must shun profane and idle babblings, whose message spreads like cancer, as seen in Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection is already past and are overthrowing the faith of some.

sections.title: God’s Firm Foundation and Vessels for Honor
sections.summary: Despite that spreading error, God’s solid foundation stands, sealed with the assurance that the Lord knows those who are His and with the call for everyone who names Christ to depart from iniquity. In a great house there are vessels for honor and for dishonor, and whoever cleanses himself “from the latter” (2 Timothy 2:21) will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful for the Master, “prepared for every good work” (2 Timothy 2:21).

sections.title: The Lord’s Servant Who Corrects with Gentleness
sections.summary: Timothy is to flee youthful lusts, pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart, and avoid foolish disputes. The Lord’s servant must not quarrel but be gentle, able to teach, and patient, correcting opponents in humility in the hope that God will grant them repentance, so that they may know the truth and escape the snare of the devil.

1.brief: Drawing a conclusion from the examples at the end of chapter 1, Paul tells Timothy, his son, to be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. The strength Timothy needs for what follows comes from Christ’s grace, not from his own resources.
1.explain:
“You therefore, my son,”

“Therefore” draws a conclusion from chapter 1. Paul has described people who turned away from him (1:15) and one man, Onesiphorus, who stood firm (1:16–18). Now he turns to Timothy: “You therefore.” The word “you” is emphatic. Whatever others have done, Timothy must take his own stand. Paul calls him “my son,” returning to the affection of 1:2. The command that follows comes from a father who loves him.

“be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.”

Timothy must “be strong.” Paul does not tell him to make himself strong by effort or willpower. He is to be strong “in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.” Grace is God’s undeserved favor, and here it is also God’s power at work in His people. The strength Timothy needs comes from Christ’s grace, not from his own resources.

The Greek verb is passive and can be understood as “be strengthened.” Timothy is to keep drawing strength from a source outside himself. Everything Paul asks in this chapter, from teaching others to enduring hardship to correcting opponents gently, depends on this grace. Without it, Timothy’s duties would crush him. With it, he can do what God has called him to do.
1.notes: The Greek verb translated “be strong” is in the passive voice and a present tense that describes ongoing action: Timothy is to keep on being strengthened. Paul uses the same verb in 4:17, where “the Lord stood with me and strengthened me.”

2.brief: What Timothy heard from Paul, confirmed among many witnesses, he must commit to faithful men who will be able to teach others also. The teaching Timothy guards must also be handed on, so that it reaches another generation of teachers.
2.explain:
“And the things that you have heard from me among many witnesses,”

Timothy has received a body of teaching. These are “the things that you have heard from me,” the gospel and the sound words Paul described in 1:13. Timothy did not receive them in secret. He heard them “among many witnesses.” Others heard the same teaching and could confirm it. Paul’s gospel was not a private message passed to an inner circle. It was public, open, and confirmed by many.

“commit these to faithful men”

Timothy must “commit these to faithful men.” The word “commit” belongs to the same family as the word Paul used in 1:12 and 1:14 for something entrusted. Timothy must guard the deposit (1:14), and he must also hand it on. Guarding the gospel does not mean locking it away. It means passing it on intact to people who will keep it.

Timothy must choose “faithful men,” people who are trustworthy and reliable. They must be faithful to the truth and faithful in character. In a time when some were turning away and false teachers were spreading error, choosing the right people mattered greatly.

“who will be able to teach others also.”

These faithful men must “be able to teach others also.” The chain of teaching reaches beyond Timothy. Paul taught Timothy, Timothy will teach faithful men, and they will teach others. That makes four generations in one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. Paul is about to die (4:6). He wants to make sure that the gospel will be handed on long after he and Timothy are gone.
2.notes:
The Greek verb translated “commit” is related to the noun used in 1:12 and 1:14 for the deposit that is entrusted and guarded. The same family of words appears in 1 Timothy 1:18, “This charge I commit to you.”

The phrase “among many witnesses” could also be read as through many witnesses, meaning that many others confirmed Paul’s teaching to Timothy. Either way, the teaching was public and confirmed by others.

“Men” translates a general Greek word for human beings. Paul’s concern is that the people entrusted with the teaching be reliable and able to teach others.

3.brief: Timothy must endure hardship as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. Paul calls him to accept suffering as part of serving under Christ’s command.
3.explain:
“You therefore must endure hardship”

“Therefore” marks a new appeal. Timothy must be strong in grace and pass on the teaching. He must also “endure hardship.” Faithful ministry will bring suffering, and Timothy must accept it rather than run from it. Paul made the same appeal in 1:8: “share with me in the sufferings for the gospel.”

“as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.”

Paul gives the first of three pictures: a “good soldier.” Soldiers expect hardship. They endure long marches, poor food, harsh conditions, and danger. They accept these as part of their service. Timothy serves in Christ’s army, and he must expect the same.

He is a soldier “of Jesus Christ.” He does not serve himself, the church, or Paul. He serves under Christ’s command. Christ is his commander, and Christ is the one he must please (2:4).
3.notes:
The Greek text behind the NKJV reads “You therefore must endure hardship.” Many other manuscripts read a verb meaning to share in suffering, the same verb used in 1:8, and translations based on them, such as the NLT, read “Endure suffering along with me.” Either way, Timothy is called to accept hardship in Christ’s service.

Paul uses military language elsewhere for Christian service. He calls coworkers “fellow soldier” (Philippians 2:25; Philemon 1:2) and charges Timothy to “wage the good warfare” (1 Timothy 1:18).

4.brief: A soldier on active service does not entangle himself with the affairs of this life, because his aim is to please the one who enlisted him. Timothy, too, must keep his attention on pleasing Christ, who called him into service.
4.explain:
“No one engaged in warfare entangles himself with the affairs of this life,”

Paul develops the soldier picture. A soldier on active duty does not get tangled up in ordinary civilian business. The word “entangles” pictures a net or snare that traps and holds back. “The affairs of this life” are the ordinary concerns of making a living, running a household, and managing business. These things are not sinful. They are simply not what a soldier on duty is there to do. A soldier who gets caught up in them cannot give his full attention to his mission.

The verse does not forbid ordinary work. Paul himself worked as a tentmaker to support himself (Acts 18:3). The point is focus. Timothy must not let ordinary concerns distract him from the mission Christ has given him.

“that he may please him who enlisted him as a soldier.”

The soldier keeps free of distractions for a reason: “that he may please him who enlisted him as a soldier.” His goal is to please his commander. Timothy’s goal is the same. Christ called him into His service, and Timothy’s highest aim is to please Christ, not to please people, gain comfort, or protect himself.
4.notes:
The Greek verb translated “entangles” appears in 2 Peter 2:20, where people are “again entangled” in the world’s pollutions. It describes being caught or wound up in something.

The Greek verb translated “enlisted him as a soldier” means to gather or recruit an army. It appears only here in the New Testament.

5.brief: An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. Faithful service must be carried out in the way the Lord requires if it is to receive His reward.
5.explain:
“And also if anyone competes in athletics,”

Paul turns to a second picture: an athlete. Athletic games were well known across the Greek and Roman world, and the Isthmian Games were held near Corinth. Timothy would have understood the picture immediately.

“he is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules.”

An athlete “is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules.” The winner received a crown, a wreath of leaves, but only if he followed the rules of the contest. An athlete who broke the rules was disqualified, no matter how fast he ran or how hard he fought.

The same is true in Christ’s service. Timothy must serve in the way the Lord requires. Success by worldly standards means nothing if it comes by compromising the truth or cutting corners. Faithful service, carried out God’s way, will receive His reward. Paul will speak of his own reward at the end of his race: “the crown of righteousness” (4:8).
5.notes:
The Greek verb translated “competes in athletics” is related to the English word “athlete.” “Crowned” translates a verb related to the noun for the victor’s wreath given at the games, the noun translated “crown” in 4:8. To be crowned was to receive that wreath as the winner.

The Greek word translated “according to the rules” means lawfully, in keeping with the rules of the contest. Ancient athletes had to meet training requirements and follow the regulations of the games.

Paul uses the same athletic picture in 1 Corinthians 9:25: “they do it to obtain a perishable crown, but we for an imperishable crown.”

6.brief: The hardworking farmer must be the first to share in the crops. The one who labors faithfully can look forward to enjoying the fruit of that labor.
6.explain:
“The hardworking farmer must be first to partake of the crops.”

The third picture is a farmer. The emphasis falls on “hardworking.” Farming demands steady, often exhausting labor: plowing, planting, weeding, watering, and harvesting. A lazy farmer gets little harvest. The hardworking farmer “must be first to partake of the crops.” The one who has labored has the first right to share in the fruit of the harvest.

Paul’s point is that faithful labor leads to reward. Timothy’s work in teaching and ministry may be long and tiring, but it is not in vain. The one who works hard for the Lord will share in the harvest. The three pictures fit together: the soldier stresses single-minded devotion, the athlete stresses obedience to the rules, and the farmer stresses steady labor. All three look forward to a reward.
6.notes:
The Greek word translated “hardworking” means to labor to the point of weariness. Paul uses the same verb for his own labor in ministry (for example, 1 Timothy 4:10, “we both labor and suffer reproach”).

Some interpreters read this verse as teaching that ministers deserve material support from those they serve, as Paul argues in 1 Corinthians 9:7–11. In this passage the emphasis falls on faithful labor and its reward, and the verse does not mention payment.

7.brief: Paul tells Timothy to consider what he has said about the soldier, the athlete, and the farmer, and he prays that the Lord will give him understanding in all things. Timothy must think the images through, while the understanding itself comes as the Lord’s gift.
7.explain:
“Consider what I say,”

Paul does not explain every detail of his three pictures. He tells Timothy to “consider” them, to think them through and work out what they mean for his ministry. Paul trusts Timothy to reflect on what he has said and apply it.

“and may the Lord give you understanding in all things.”

Thinking is Timothy’s part, but understanding is the Lord’s gift. Paul prays that “the Lord” will “give you understanding in all things.” Careful thought and dependence on God belong together. Timothy must use his mind, and he must look to the Lord to grant insight. Neither replaces the other.
7.notes:
The Greek text behind the NKJV reads “may the Lord give you understanding.” Many other manuscripts read a promise that the Lord will give understanding, rather than a prayer. Both readings agree that understanding comes from the Lord.

The Greek verb translated “consider” means to think about something carefully, to reflect on it and grasp its meaning.

8.brief: Paul calls Timothy to remember that Jesus Christ, of the seed of David, was raised from the dead according to Paul’s gospel. Christ’s descent from David ties Him to God’s promises to David’s line, and His resurrection stands at the center of the message Timothy must hold.
8.explain:
“Remember that Jesus Christ,”

Paul now gives Timothy the center of the gospel to hold onto. “Remember.” In the middle of hardship, Timothy must keep Jesus Christ before his mind. Remembering is more than recalling facts. It means keeping Christ at the center of his thoughts and drawing strength from who He is and what He has done.

“of the seed of David,”

Jesus is “of the seed of David.” He descended from King David. God had promised David that one of his descendants would reign on his throne forever (2 Samuel 7:12–16). Jesus is that descendant. By naming David, Paul reminds Timothy that the gospel is the fulfillment of God’s ancient promises. Jesus is the promised King.

His descent from David also points to His full humanity. Jesus was a real man, born into a real family line. He suffered as a man and died as a man, which makes Him able to understand and help those who suffer.

“was raised from the dead”

Jesus “was raised from the dead.” This is the heart of the gospel. Jesus died and rose again. His resurrection proves that He is who He claimed to be, that His sacrifice was accepted, and that death has been defeated (1:10). For Timothy, who faced suffering and possibly death, the resurrection was the ground of hope. If Jesus rose, then those who belong to Him will rise too. This matters all the more in this chapter, because some false teachers were saying the resurrection had already happened (2:18).

“according to my gospel,”

This is “my gospel,” the gospel Paul preached. Paul does not mean that he invented it. He means it was the gospel entrusted to him, the message he proclaimed and for which he suffered. It was the same gospel he had handed to Timothy.
8.notes:
The Greek verb translated “was raised” describes a completed act with continuing results: Jesus was raised, and He remains the risen One.

Paul uses the phrase “according to my gospel” in Romans 2:16 and Romans 16:25 as well.

Paul names David’s line and the resurrection together at the opening of Romans, where Jesus Christ is “born of the seed of David according to the flesh” and declared to be the Son of God with power “by the resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:3–4).

9.brief: For that gospel Paul suffers trouble as if he were an evildoer, even to the point of chains. Yet “the word of God is not chained,” and the message keeps advancing while its messenger is bound.
9.explain:
“for which I suffer trouble as an evildoer, even to the point of chains;”

Paul suffers “for” the gospel, because of it. He says, “I suffer trouble as an evildoer.” The word “evildoer” means a criminal, someone who commits serious crimes. Paul is being treated like a common criminal, not because he has done wrong, but because he preaches Christ. It is the shame Paul urged Timothy not to fear (1:8).

His suffering goes “even to the point of chains.” Paul is literally bound. This is the reality of his situation in Rome.

“but the word of God is not chained.”

“But” brings a triumphant contrast. Paul is chained, but “the word of God is not chained.” The messenger can be bound, but the message cannot. While Paul sits in prison, the gospel continues to spread through others, through his letters, and through the testimony of his suffering. No prison can stop God’s word from doing its work.

This was encouraging for Timothy. Paul’s chains might make it seem as if the gospel was losing ground. Paul assures him otherwise. God’s word is still free and still advancing.
9.notes:
The Greek word translated “evildoer” is the same word Luke uses for the criminals crucified with Jesus (Luke 23:32, “two others, criminals”). Paul’s treatment as a criminal resembles his Lord’s.

The Greek verb translated “is not chained” is the passive form of the verb for binding, and the word for “chains” earlier in the verse comes from the same root. Paul’s wording sets the two side by side: Paul wears chains, but the word of God is not bound.

10.brief: Therefore Paul endures all things for the sake of the elect, the people God has chosen, so that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory. His suffering serves the salvation of others.
10.explain:
“Therefore I endure all things for the sake of the elect,”

“Therefore” points back to the unchained word. Because God’s word is still at work, Paul’s suffering is not wasted. He can say, “I endure all things,” bearing up under hardship without giving up. He does it “for the sake of the elect.” The elect are the people God has chosen. Paul suffers so that they may be reached and strengthened.

God’s choosing does not make Paul’s work unnecessary. Paul knows that God has chosen people, and that is exactly why he labors and endures. God uses the preaching of the gospel and the faithfulness of His servants to bring His chosen ones to salvation.

“that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus”

Paul’s goal is “that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus.” He wants others to receive the salvation he has received. Salvation is “in Christ Jesus.” It is found only in union with Him.

“with eternal glory.”

This salvation comes “with eternal glory.” It includes not only rescue from sin now but the glory of God’s presence forever. Present suffering is temporary. The glory that follows is eternal. Paul endures now because he knows what is coming for those who belong to Christ.
10.notes:
The Greek verb translated “endure” is related to the word used in 2:12 (“If we endure”). It means to remain under a burden, bearing it patiently without giving up.

The Greek word translated “elect” means chosen ones. Paul uses the same word in Titus 1:1, “according to the faith of God’s elect.”

11.brief: Paul introduces a faithful, trustworthy saying that begins with a promise: if we died with Christ, we shall also live with Him. Those who share in His death will share in His risen life.
11.explain:
“This is a faithful saying:”

Paul introduces a “faithful saying,” a trustworthy statement. This phrase appears several times in Paul’s letters to Timothy and Titus, always to mark a statement that can be fully relied on. The saying that follows has four lines, each beginning with “if.” The four lines belong together and must be read as one whole. Two lines promise, one warns, and the last rests everything on Christ’s faithfulness.

“For if we died with Him,”

The first line looks back to the believer’s union with Christ in His death. “If we died with Him” describes what happened when a person came to faith in Christ. Believers share in Christ’s death. Their old life under sin and self has come to an end. Paul taught the same truth in Romans 6:8: “Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Him.”

In the setting of this letter, the words may also include dying for Christ’s sake. Paul expects to be executed soon (4:6). For him, dying with Christ was about to become very literal. Whether the death is spiritual or physical, the promise is the same.

“We shall also live with Him.”

The promise follows: “We shall also live with Him.” Those who share in Christ’s death will share in His risen life. Death is not the end for those who belong to Christ. They will live with Him now and forever. This is the hope that makes suffering for the gospel bearable.
11.notes:
“This is a faithful saying” occurs five times in the Pastoral Letters (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). In each case it marks a statement of special importance.

The Greek verb translated “died with” describes a completed act. It points to a decisive death with Christ rather than a continuing process.

The lines of 2:11–13 have a balanced, rhythmic form, and many scholars think they may come from an early Christian hymn or confession. The NKJV prints them as poetry.

12.brief: The saying continues with a second promise, that those who endure will also reign with Christ, and then a warning: “If we deny Him, He also will deny us.” Read with the whole saying, the warning concerns a settled, final denial of Christ, which meets His denial.
12.explain:
“If we endure, We shall also reign with Him.”

The second line promises reward for faithfulness. “If we endure” means continuing to stand firm under hardship and pressure, without giving up. Paul has just said that he endures all things (2:10). Timothy is called to endure as well (2:3).

The promise is “We shall also reign with Him.” Those who endure will share in Christ’s rule when His kingdom comes in fullness. Suffering now leads to reigning later. Believers who endure are not crushed by their trials. They are on their way to the throne.

“If we deny Him, He also will deny us.”

The third line is a serious warning. “If we deny Him” means to disown Christ, to refuse to acknowledge Him as Lord, to turn away from Him. Jesus Himself said, “But whoever denies Me before men, him I will also deny before My Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:33).

The consequence is solemn: “He also will deny us.” Christ will not acknowledge as His own those who have finally disowned Him. Read with the whole saying, this warning concerns a settled, final denial of Christ, a turning away that is never repented of. Christ means what He says, and the warning must be heard at full weight.

The Gospels show the difference between a fall and a final denial. Peter denied Jesus three times, yet he repented, wept bitterly, and was restored by the risen Lord (Luke 22:31–32; John 21:15–17). Judas betrayed Jesus and did not return (Matthew 26:47–50; 27:3–5). Peter’s story shows that a believer who falls still has room to repent. The warning in this line concerns those who finally and lastingly deny Christ. It is not meant to drive struggling believers to despair, and it does not give anyone permission to treat denial lightly.
12.notes:
The two conditions use different verb forms in Greek. “If we endure” describes continuing endurance. “If we deny” is in a future tense in many manuscripts, looking ahead to a possible act of denial. The tense alone does not show that the denial is final; that reading comes from the saying as a whole and from Jesus’ words in Matthew 10:33.

The Greek verb translated “deny” is the same word used in Matthew 10:33 and in the accounts of Peter’s denial (for example, Matthew 26:72, “But again he denied with an oath”).

13.brief: The last line says that if we are faithless, He remains faithful, because He cannot deny Himself. The saying rests on Christ’s unchanging character, so that He stays true both to His promises and to His warning.
13.explain:
“If we are faithless,”

The fourth line is the most surprising. “If we are faithless” means to be unfaithful, to fail in trust or loyalty. The Greek word can mean either disbelieving or being unfaithful. The line names failure toward Christ without saying how far it goes, and the rest of the line shows why the saying carries both comfort and warning.

“He remains faithful;”

The answer is “He remains faithful.” Christ’s faithfulness does not depend on ours. He keeps His word whether we are strong or weak. This line rests the whole saying on Christ’s unchanging character. He will keep His promises to those who died with Him and endure (2:11–12). He will also keep His warning to those who finally deny Him (2:12).

“He cannot deny Himself.”

The reason is that “He cannot deny Himself.” Christ cannot act against His own nature or break His own word. If He promised life to those who trust Him, He will give it. If He warned of judgment for those who deny Him, that warning stands. His faithfulness guarantees both the promise and the warning.

This line gives hope to a believer who has stumbled. Christ’s faithfulness is stronger than our failures. He does not abandon His people when they waver. But it also guards against careless confidence. Christ’s faithfulness does not mean He will ignore final denial. He remains true to everything He has said.
13.notes:
The Greek verb translated “are faithless” is built from the word for faith with a negative prefix. The setting, a saying about loyalty to Christ, favors the sense of unfaithfulness here.

Interpreters have read this line in two main ways: as a promise that Christ keeps His own when they fail, or as a reinforcement of the warning in 2:12. The four-line arrangement helps explain why both readings arise. In the first three lines, what we do is answered by a matching result. This line breaks the pattern: our faithlessness is not answered by His faithlessness. The reason given, “He cannot deny Himself,” points to Christ’s own character rather than to a matching reward or penalty.

The phrase “He cannot deny Himself” echoes the Old Testament conviction that God does not lie or go back on His word (for example, Numbers 23:19; Titus 1:2).

14.brief: Timothy must remind those he teaches of these things and charge them before the Lord not to strive about words. Such quarrels profit no one and bring ruin to those who listen.
14.explain:
“Remind them of these things,”

Paul turns to Timothy’s ministry among others. Timothy must “remind them of these things.” The word “them” most likely refers to the faithful men of 2:2 and to the church Timothy serves. “These things” are the truths Paul has just given, especially the faithful saying in 2:11–13. Believers need constant reminding of what they already know.

“charging them before the Lord”

Timothy must charge them “before the Lord.” This is a solemn command given in the Lord’s presence. It reminds everyone that they answer to Christ for how they handle His truth.

“not to strive about words to no profit,”

The charge is “not to strive about words.” This describes fighting over words, arguing about terms, phrases, or fine distinctions in ways that lead nowhere. The false teachers in Ephesus loved this kind of debate. Paul says it is “to no profit.” It does not build anyone up, deepen faith, or advance the gospel.

“to the ruin of the hearers.”

Worse, word fights lead “to the ruin of the hearers.” The people who listen to such quarrels are harmed. They become confused, unsettled, or drawn away from simple faith in Christ. Paul wants Timothy to protect believers from teaching that tears them down.
14.notes:
The Greek text behind the NKJV reads “before the Lord.” Many other manuscripts read “before God,” and the NLT reads “in God’s presence.” Either way, the charge is given in the presence of the One to whom all will answer.

The Greek verb translated “strive about words” is a compound of “word” and “fight.” A related noun appears in 1 Timothy 6:4, where false teachers are “obsessed with disputes and arguments over words.”

The Greek word translated “ruin” means overthrow or destruction. It is related to the English word “catastrophe.”

15.brief: Timothy must be diligent to present himself approved to God, a worker who does not need to be ashamed, “rightly dividing the word of truth.” He is to handle God’s word accurately and faithfully, the way a careful worker does a job he can stand behind.
15.explain:
“Be diligent to present yourself approved to God,”

In contrast to word fighters, Timothy must “be diligent.” The word means to make every effort, to be eager and earnest. He must work hard at his ministry.

His goal is to “present yourself approved to God.” “Approved” describes something tested and found genuine, like metal that has been tried and proven pure. Timothy’s aim is not to win arguments or impress people. He seeks God’s approval.

“a worker who does not need to be ashamed,”

Timothy must be “a worker who does not need to be ashamed.” A good worker does his job so well that he can stand behind it. When his work is inspected, he has nothing to hide. Timothy must labor in God’s word so faithfully that he will not be ashamed when his work is examined by God.

“rightly dividing the word of truth.”

The phrase “rightly dividing” means to handle accurately, to cut straight. The picture is of a craftsman cutting a straight line or a road builder making a straight path. Timothy must handle “the word of truth” with care and accuracy, teaching it correctly and applying it rightly. He must not twist it, distort it, or use it for his own purposes. The phrase does not mean splitting the Bible into separate parts. It means handling the whole of God’s word faithfully.

This stands in sharp contrast to the false teachers. They fought over words and twisted the truth. Timothy must handle the word straight.
15.notes:
The Greek word translated “approved” describes something tested and proven genuine. Its opposite, “disapproved,” describes the false teachers in 3:8.

The Greek verb translated “rightly dividing” means to cut straight. It occurs only here in the New Testament. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament it is used in Proverbs 3:6 and Proverbs 11:5 for making a path straight.

16.brief: Timothy must shun profane and idle babblings, for they will increase to more ungodliness. Empty religious talk is not harmless, because it carries people further from God.
16.explain:
“But shun profane and idle babblings,”

Timothy must “shun” a certain kind of talk. The word means to turn away from, to avoid. He must keep away from “profane and idle babblings.” “Profane” means common or godless, without any sacred character. “Idle babblings” means empty chatter, words without substance. The false teachers produced plenty of talk that sounded religious but had nothing of God in it.

“for they will increase to more ungodliness.”

Paul gives the reason: “they will increase to more ungodliness.” Empty religious talk is not harmless. It does not stay still. It progresses, but in the wrong direction. Those who indulge in it move further and further from God. What begins as curiosity or clever argument ends in godlessness.
16.notes:
Paul uses the same phrase in 1 Timothy 6:20: “avoiding the profane and idle babblings.”

The Greek verb translated “will increase” means to advance or make progress. Paul uses it with irony here, since the false teachers advance only into ungodliness. The same verb appears in 3:9 (“they will progress no further”) and 3:13 (“will grow worse and worse”).

17.brief: The message of such talk spreads like cancer, eating away at the health of the church. Paul names Hymenaeus and Philetus as examples of men who teach this way.
17.explain:
“And their message will spread like cancer.”

Paul describes the effect of this talk. “Their message will spread like cancer.” The word refers to a spreading sore that eats away at healthy flesh. Once it takes hold, it keeps spreading and destroying. False teaching works the same way. It spreads from person to person, eating away at the health of the church.

The picture contrasts with the “sound words” of 1:13. Sound teaching produces spiritual health. False teaching spreads disease.

“Hymenaeus and Philetus are of this sort,”

Paul names two men who spread this kind of teaching: Hymenaeus and Philetus. Naming them was a warning to Timothy and the church. These were real people, and their influence was real. A Hymenaeus is also named in 1 Timothy 1:20, where Paul says he delivered Hymenaeus and Alexander to Satan “that they may learn not to blaspheme.” If this is the same man, he continued spreading error after Paul’s earlier discipline. Philetus is not mentioned anywhere else.
17.notes:
The Greek word translated “cancer” is the word from which English gets “gangrene.” It describes a spreading infection that destroys living tissue.

The Greek phrase behind “will spread” reads literally will have pasture, a picture of a spreading sore feeding on the flesh around it.

18.brief: These men have strayed concerning the truth by saying that the resurrection is already past, and they are overthrowing the faith of some. Denying the future resurrection undermines the hope on which faith rests.
18.explain:
“who have strayed concerning the truth,”

Hymenaeus and Philetus “have strayed concerning the truth.” The word means to miss the mark or to wander off course. They once held to the truth, or at least appeared to, but they had drifted away.

“saying that the resurrection is already past;”

Their error was specific: “saying that the resurrection is already past.” They taught that there would be no future bodily resurrection, because the resurrection had already happened. Paul reports only their claim, not how they reached it. Some interpreters suggest they spoke of a spiritual resurrection already experienced, perhaps at conversion or baptism, but the text does not say so. What Paul makes clear is that the claim set aside the resurrection still to come.

This was a serious error. Paul had just told Timothy to remember that Jesus Christ was raised from the dead (2:8). The resurrection of Christ guarantees the future resurrection of believers (1 Corinthians 15:20). To deny the future resurrection undermines the whole hope of the gospel.

“and they overthrow the faith of some.”

The result was that “they overthrow the faith of some.” Their teaching was not merely mistaken. It was destructive. People who accepted it were losing their faith. When the hope of resurrection is removed, faith loses its foundation. Paul names this error because it was doing real damage to real people.
18.notes:
The Greek verb translated “have strayed” means to miss the mark. Paul uses it in 1 Timothy 1:6 and 1 Timothy 6:21 for people who have strayed from the truth.

Paul faced a related problem in Corinth, where some said “there is no resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:12). The error at Ephesus seems to have been different: it did not deny resurrection outright but claimed it had already taken place.

The Greek verb translated “overthrow” means to upset or turn upside down. Jesus overturned the money changers’ tables in the temple (John 2:15), and the same verb is used there.

19.brief: Nevertheless, God’s solid foundation stands, bearing a seal with two inscriptions: “The Lord knows those who are His,” and “Let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity.” God’s knowledge of His own gives security, and turning from iniquity marks those who belong to Him.
19.explain:
“Nevertheless the solid foundation of God stands,”

“Nevertheless” brings hope after the bad news of 2:17–18. Some people’s faith is being overthrown, but “the solid foundation of God stands.” God’s foundation is firm and unshaken. False teachers can unsettle individuals, but they cannot destroy what God has built.

The verse does not say exactly what the “foundation” is. It is most often understood as the church, God’s people whom He has established and who rest on Christ. Others take it as God’s truth or God’s work of salvation. Each reading points to the same reality: what God has built stands secure.

“having this seal:”

The foundation bears a “seal.” In the ancient world, a seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity. Inscriptions were sometimes carved on a building’s foundation stones. God’s foundation has two inscriptions.

“The Lord knows those who are His,”

The first inscription is “The Lord knows those who are His.” These words recall Numbers 16:5, where Moses said, “Tomorrow morning the LORD will show who is His and who is holy.” In that story, Korah and his followers rebelled against Moses and Aaron, and God made clear who truly belonged to Him.

For Timothy, this was a great comfort. False teachers might confuse many, but the Lord knows His own. He is not confused about who belongs to Him. No error can snatch His people from Him. Their security rests on His knowledge of them, not on their own grasp of the truth.

“and, “Let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity.””

The second inscription balances the first: “Let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity.” Those who claim to belong to Christ must turn away from sin. In Numbers 16 Moses told the people to “Depart now from the tents of these wicked men!” (Numbers 16:26). Those who belong to the Lord separate themselves from evil.

The two inscriptions belong together. God knows His people, which gives them security. His people turn from iniquity, which gives evidence that they belong to Him. Both sides are true. God’s knowledge comes first, and holy living follows. In the setting of this chapter, departing from iniquity includes turning away from the false teaching of 2:16–18.
19.notes:
The first inscription closely matches the Greek translation of Numbers 16:5, which reads, in English, God knew those who are His. The second inscription is not a direct quotation. It draws on Old Testament language such as Numbers 16:26 and Isaiah 52:11 (“Depart! Depart! Go out from there, Touch no unclean thing”).

The Greek text behind the NKJV reads “the name of Christ.” Many other manuscripts read the Lord in place of Christ, and the NLT reads “All who belong to the LORD.” The meaning is the same.

The Greek word translated “seal” refers to the mark of ownership pressed into wax or clay, or the inscription carved on a stone. It marked something as belonging to its owner and authenticated it.

20.brief: Paul pictures a great house that has vessels of gold and silver and also of wood and clay, some for honor and some for dishonor. Even in a large household, not every vessel is fit for honorable use.
20.explain:
“But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay,”

Paul uses a new picture. In “a great house,” a large household of a wealthy family, there were many kinds of “vessels,” containers, dishes, and utensils. Some were made of “gold and silver,” valuable and beautiful. Others were made of “wood and clay,” cheap and ordinary.

The “great house” represents the visible church, God’s household. In the church, as in a large house, there are different kinds of people. Some are faithful and devoted. Others are not.

“some for honor and some for dishonor.”

The vessels serve different purposes: “some for honor and some for dishonor.” Gold and silver vessels were used for honorable purposes, such as serving guests at a banquet. Wood and clay vessels might be used for dishonorable purposes, such as carrying garbage or waste.

In context, the vessels for dishonor include the false teachers like Hymenaeus and Philetus. They were in the church but were not fit for honorable use. The vessels for honor are those who serve God faithfully. The picture prepares for 2:21, where Paul shows how a person becomes a vessel for honor.
20.notes:
The Greek word translated “vessels” refers to any container, dish, or utensil used in a household. Paul uses the same word in 2 Corinthians 4:7, “we have this treasure in earthen vessels,” and in Romans 9:21 for vessels for honor and dishonor.

Paul’s first letter calls the church “the house of God” (1 Timothy 3:15). The great house in this verse fits that picture.

21.brief: Therefore if anyone cleanses himself “from the latter,” he will be a vessel for honor, sanctified and useful for the Master, “prepared for every good work.” In context this cleansing includes departing from the iniquity named in 2:19 and rejecting the corrupt teaching of 2:16–18, and the one who does so is set apart for the Master’s use and ready for whatever He wants to do through him.
21.explain:
“Therefore if anyone cleanses himself from the latter,”

“Therefore” draws a practical conclusion. “If anyone cleanses himself from the latter” means separating oneself from what is dishonorable. “The latter” refers to the vessels for dishonor in 2:20. In context, cleansing includes departing from the iniquity named in 2:19 and rejecting the corrupt teaching of 2:16–18. A person must separate himself from false teaching and from sin.

The verse says “cleanses himself.” A person has responsibility to turn from what is dishonorable. This does not mean that a person earns God’s favor. It means that those who belong to the Lord actively turn from iniquity (2:19).

“he will be a vessel for honor,”

The result is that “he will be a vessel for honor.” A person who cleanses himself becomes fit for honorable use in God’s household. God uses clean vessels for His purposes.

“sanctified and useful for the Master,”

Such a vessel is “sanctified,” set apart for God’s use. It belongs to the Master and is reserved for His purposes. It is also “useful for the Master.” God can use it for His work. The “Master” is the Lord, the head of the household.

“prepared for every good work.”

Finally, such a vessel is “prepared for every good work.” It is ready for whatever the Master wants to do through it. A clean vessel is not only kept from what is wrong. It is ready for what is good. Paul will return to this idea in 3:17, where Scripture makes the man of God “thoroughly equipped for every good work.”
21.notes:
The Greek verb translated “cleanses himself” means to clean out thoroughly. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 5:7: “Therefore purge out the old leaven.”

The Greek phrase behind “from the latter” reads literally “from these.” It most naturally refers to the vessels for dishonor in 2:20, though some take it as the false teaching and teachers of 2:16–18. Both are in view in this passage.

The Greek word translated “useful” is the word Paul uses for Mark in 4:11 (“useful to me for ministry”) and for Onesimus in Philemon 1:11 (“profitable”).

The Greek word translated “Master” refers to an owner with authority over the household and its servants. It is a different word from the usual word for “Lord.”

22.brief: Timothy must flee youthful lusts and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace together with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart. Holiness means both running from what corrupts and pursuing godliness alongside other sincere believers.
22.explain:
“Flee also youthful lusts;”

Paul turns to Timothy’s own life. “Flee” means to run away, to escape. Some things must not be fought, debated, or managed. They must be fled.

Timothy must flee “youthful lusts.” These are the desires that especially tempt younger people. Sexual desire is included, but the phrase is broader. It also covers impatience, love of argument, pride, desire for recognition, and a quickness to fight over words. Timothy was not a teenager. He was probably in his thirties when Paul wrote. Yet in the ancient world he was still considered relatively young for a leader (compare 1 Timothy 4:12). The surrounding verses suggest that the youthful desires Paul has in mind include the love of controversy that fed the false teaching.

“but pursue righteousness, faith, love, peace”

Fleeing is only half of the command. Timothy must also “pursue.” He must run toward something good.

He must pursue “righteousness,” living in a way that is right before God and people. He must pursue “faith,” trust in God and faithfulness to Him. He must pursue “love,” care for God and for others. He must pursue “peace,” harmony with God and with others instead of quarrels and division. These qualities are the opposite of what the false teachers produced.

“with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.”

Timothy must pursue these things “with those who call on the Lord out of a pure heart.” He is not to pursue godliness alone. He must do it alongside other sincere believers. To “call on the Lord” means to pray to Him and worship Him. A “pure heart” is a heart without hidden motives, sincere and undivided toward God. Paul’s first letter gave the same aim for all his instruction: “love from a pure heart, from a good conscience, and from sincere faith” (1 Timothy 1:5).
22.notes: Paul gives Timothy a similar command in 1 Timothy 6:11: “flee these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, gentleness.”

23.brief: Timothy must avoid foolish and ignorant disputes, knowing that they generate strife. Paul separates necessary correction from pointless arguments that only produce quarrels.
23.explain:
“But avoid foolish and ignorant disputes,”

Timothy must “avoid” certain kinds of debates. The word means to refuse, to have nothing to do with. He must avoid “foolish and ignorant disputes.” “Foolish” describes debates that lack wisdom and sense. “Ignorant” describes debates carried on by people who do not really understand what they are talking about. Such debates are pointless.

Paul does not forbid all discussion or correction. He will tell Timothy in the next verses how to correct those in opposition (2:25). What Paul forbids is getting caught up in useless arguments that go nowhere.

“knowing that they generate strife.”

Timothy should avoid these disputes “knowing that they generate strife.” Foolish debates produce quarrels and conflict. They do not produce understanding, faith, or love. Timothy should recognize them for what they are and stay clear.
23.notes:
The Greek word translated “ignorant” means uninstructed or untrained. It describes debates that come from a lack of real understanding.

The Greek word translated “strife” means fights or battles. It appears in the plural, suggesting repeated quarrels.

24.brief: A servant of the Lord must not quarrel but be gentle to all, able to teach, and patient. The manner of his ministry must reflect the Lord he serves.
24.explain:
“And a servant of the Lord must not quarrel”

Timothy is “a servant of the Lord.” The word means a slave, one who belongs to his master and serves him. Timothy belongs to the Lord and serves Him. That shapes how he must behave.

A servant of the Lord “must not quarrel.” He must not be argumentative or combative. He must not fight to win, defend his pride, or crush opponents. This was the opposite of the false teachers, who loved quarrels.

“but be gentle to all,”

Instead, the Lord’s servant must “be gentle to all.” “Gentle” means kind, mild, and patient in dealing with people. A nurse caring for a sick child shows the same kind of gentleness. Timothy must be gentle “to all,” not only to friends but also to opponents and difficult people.

“able to teach,”

He must also be “able to teach.” Gentleness does not mean silence. The Lord’s servant must be skilled in explaining God’s truth clearly. Teaching is one of his main tools for helping people.

“patient,”

Finally, he must be “patient.” The Greek word describes bearing evil without resentment, putting up with wrongs without growing bitter. People will oppose, misunderstand, and hurt the Lord’s servant. He must not retaliate. He must patiently keep doing good.
24.notes:
The Greek word translated “able to teach” appears also in 1 Timothy 3:2 as a requirement for overseers.

The Greek word translated “patient” appears only here in the New Testament. It is formed from words meaning “to bear” and “evil.”

25.brief: The Lord’s servant must correct those in opposition with humility, in the hope that God perhaps will grant them repentance so that they may know the truth. Repentance is God’s gift, and patient correction aims at the opponent’s recovery.
25.explain:
“in humility correcting those who are in opposition,”

The Lord’s servant must correct, but he must do it “in humility.” The word describes gentleness and meekness, a strength that is held under control. Timothy is not to be harsh or arrogant. He corrects people as someone who also depends on God’s grace.

He must correct “those who are in opposition,” people who resist the truth and set themselves against it. The word “correcting” means to instruct, to train, to bring someone back to the right way. The goal of correction is restoration, not humiliation.

“if God perhaps will grant them repentance,”

The reason for gentle correction is hope: “if God perhaps will grant them repentance.” “Repentance” means a change of mind and heart that turns a person from error to truth. Repentance is God’s gift. The Lord’s servant cannot force it, argue it into existence, or produce it by clever debate. Only God can grant it.

The word “perhaps” shows that the outcome is not guaranteed. Some opponents may never repent. But the Lord’s servant must keep hoping and keep correcting gently, because God may yet grant them repentance.

“so that they may know the truth,”

The aim of repentance is “that they may know the truth.” Opponents who repent come to recognize and accept the truth they had rejected. This is the goal of all Timothy’s correction: not to win an argument but to see people come to the truth.
25.notes:
The Greek verb translated “correcting” is the verb used for training and educating children. Paul uses a related noun in 3:16 for “instruction in righteousness.”

The Greek phrase behind “know the truth” uses a word for full knowledge. Paul uses the same phrase in 3:7, where certain people are “never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

26.brief: Paul hopes that those in opposition may come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil, who has taken them captive to do his will. Those who oppose the truth are pictured as captives who need rescue.
26.explain:
“and that they may come to their senses”

Paul adds another hope: “that they may come to their senses.” The Greek word describes sobering up after being drunk. Those in opposition are like people intoxicated by error. Their thinking is clouded. Paul hopes they will wake up and see clearly again.

“and escape the snare of the devil,”

Paul hopes they will “escape the snare of the devil.” A “snare” is a trap. The devil had set a trap, and those in opposition had fallen into it. False teaching is not only intellectual error. It is spiritual bondage. Behind the human teachers stands a real enemy who seeks to deceive and destroy.

“having been taken captive by him to do his will.”

Those in opposition have been “taken captive by him to do his will.” They are not free. They are prisoners of the devil, doing his will instead of God’s. This changes how Timothy should view them. They are not simply enemies to be defeated. They are captives who need rescue. That is why gentleness and patience matter so much. Timothy is not fighting people. He is seeking to free them.
26.notes:
The Greek verb translated “come to their senses” appears only here in the New Testament.

The Greek verb translated “taken captive” means to capture alive. Jesus uses the same verb when He tells Simon, “From now on you will catch men” (Luke 5:10).

The Greek text uses two different pronouns in the phrase “by him to do his will,” which has led to more than one reading. The NKJV takes both to refer to the devil, who holds people captive to do his will. Some interpreters take the second pronoun to refer to God, so that those who escape the devil’s snare are then brought to do God’s will. The NKJV reading is the most natural, and the verse’s main point is the same either way: those in opposition need rescue.
